These Little Town Blues BY JOE FORDHAM H luman overpopulation has fascinated science fiction writers from Aldous Huxley to Kurt Vonnegut and perhaps most famously Harry Harrison, whose 1966 novel Make Room! Make Room! inspired the 1973 film Soylent Green, which proposed grim solutions to future urban blight. More recently, Blade Runner, WALL-E and Elysium offered scenarios in which the rich and privileged vacated a dying planet. Filmmaker Alexander Payne and co-writer Jim Taylor - known for their satirical indie dramas Election and Sideways - had a more whimsical proposition in Paramount Pictures' Downsizing. Payne and Taylor imagined a procedure that permitted living organisms to be reduced in mass by a ratio of 2,744:1. Norwegian scientist, Doctor Jorgen Asbjørnsen (Rolf Lassgård), shrinks himself to 12.9-centimeters - approximately five inches tall - and astounds the scientific community. Ten years later, Omaha residents Paul and Audrey Safranek (Matt Damon and Kristen Wiig) marvel at TV reports of Asbjørnsen's 'downsizing' program, and become intrigued with the idea of consolidating their assets by committing to the shrinking process. After liquidating their mortgage, Paul and Audrey uproot 1 / 29 to Leisureland, a utopian oasis of 1/14-scale luxury-living in New Mexico, which promises

a life of seemingly limitless miniature bounty. DOWNSIZING To investigate techniques for filming miniaturized characters, Payne met with visual effects supervisor James Price in 2009, seven years before the project came to fruition. It was interesting to compare my first breakdown with what we ended up shooting much later," noted Jamie Price. "Recently, there have been a lot of advances in digital doubles and other digital technologies, but this remained a performance-based movie that used a photographic approach. We wanted to use visual effects for creating environments and interactions between normal-sized and miniaturized people, pulling the camera back to create illusions of scale, but Alexander always wanted to rely on live-action performances. The filmmakers researched Farciot Edouart and Gordon Jennings' optical work on Paramount's 1940 Dr. Cyclops and Peter Ellenshaw's forced-perspective illusions in Disney's 1959 Darby O'Gill and the Little People.iThere were shrunken people scenes in Bride of Frankenstein, The Incredible Shrinking Man and in more recent movies," noted Price. Most often, we found shrinking scenes fell into a few different genres - fantasies, family movies, science-fiction movies or comedies. Tonally and textually, none of those were the movie that Alexander wanted to make. Alexander asked me, 'What movie would you say is most like what we're trying to achieve?' There really wasn't an example - but that gave us an opportunity to take an idea that's been around for a long time and give it a fresh look." "What was interesting about our film was that it did not have much to do with previous shrinking people films," agreed visual effects producer Susan MacLeod, who joined 2 / 29 preproduction on the Paramount Studios lot in 2015. "Previous films had been very gim-

micky about shrinking effects. Our movie was more about the social concept of how the downsizing process enabled characters to live different lives. Our goal was to believably facilitate those story points, rather than draw attention to how cool it was that characters were small.i A off the effects was meticulous planning," said MacLeod. "Sometimes, we had less than a day between shooting the 'big' and 'small' sides of a scene. Previs was super helpful in planning those interactions." "Alexander had not worked with previs before," noted The Third Floor previsualization supervisor Jourdan Biziou. "It was important to make him feel comfortable with the process. Working with Jamie, we started with some wonderful storyboards that an artist named Michael Jackson created, and we translated those into 3D stills. Alexander experimented with his choice of lenses - he's fond of wide lenses, and likes to see everything in a frame - and we honed in on the particulars of environments, what the characters were doing and their placements in scenes before we got into the technical parameters of how big/small scenes could be filmed." Downsizing concepts took into account the science behind shrinking, and the filmmakers consulted with a physicist to learn how downsizing might plausibly be done.iOne idea involved shrinking atoms and the space between them,i commented Jamie Price. DOWNSIZING s logistics and casting details took shape, the visual effects team worked with production designer Stefania Cella to plan locations and set builds using previsualizations initiated at The Third Floor. The key consideration in pulling 3 / 29

¿Another was to think of the process as removing atoms; and that was the theory we deDOWNSIZING cided would underpin the technology. But we walked a line between reminding the audience that characters were small without that getting in the way. For example, we considered what happens when a downsized person gets sad - do they have to pull a big teardrop out of their eye? The answer to that was 'no.' Yet, we decided the water in the Leisureland marina should appear human scale, so boats appeared small. We took dramatic license, using downsized effects selectively to bring the audience into the feeling of this world without constantly distracting them from the drama. The filmmakers limited juxtapositions of actors with oversized props to key scenes, including Paul's first encounter with a downsized person when he engages his college buddy, Dave Johnson (Jason Sudeikis), in a kitchen conversation while Dave perches on a cracker box. We sat Jason on an oversized cracker box so that we would get all the bounce light and proper interactions," Price explained. "We then rotoscoped Jason from the plate and used a real-sized cracker box in our composite. Generally, we knew we weren't going to be relighting digital characters, so whenever we shot a greenscreen element, we prioritized lighting on the characters and opted to rotoscope." Downsized scenes required appropriately scaled lighting reference.iWe did an interesting twist on a classic visual effects technique. We had a small gray/chrome ball and a 14-times-bigger version. Whenever we were shooting a scene that required a small person to be inserted, we put in the small, gray ball. When we lit the greenscreen for the downsized element, we pulled the camera back, placed the 14-times-bigger gray ball into the scene, mixed 4 / 29 that with the original background plate and adjusted lighting until the gray balls matched.

DOWNSIZING That way, we knew that characters would match with our composite." ndustrial Light & Magic joined the production to develop the look of downsizing effects.iJamie and Alexander made a conscious decision not to go with a shallow depth-of-field miniature look,i noted ILM visual effects supervisor Lindy De Quattro. ¿That played into the conceit that when we were shooting in the normal human world, there was a big camera person operating a big camera. When we were in a small world, we imagined the camera operator was a small person using a small camera, hence all the optics would be identical to a big person shooting with a big camera. The filmmakers shot background plates for 'big/small' scenes in multiple passes, varying focus from foreground to background, averaging f11 at three frames per second, and then selected focal distance during the composite. "We selected focus distance depending on who was operating the camera - if we adopted the point of view of a big person in the big world looking at a small person, we composited the little person with a shallow depth of field. If we had a small person looking up at a big person, we used a small camera and the focal length was longer. At first, it was a little bit confusing, but once we got into the swing of it, there was a logic behind it.i ILM outsourced some work to Rodeo FX, Whiskytree and Base FX, and the filmmakers apportioned other sequences to Framestore, Shade VFA, Atomic Fiction and Lola VFX. Halon and Mr. X joined The Third Floor in previsualizing downsized scenes, which included those within the film's most challenging environment of Leisureland. Alexander 5 / 29 felt that Leisureland should be spectacularly banal," stated Jamie Price. "We tried to

DOWNSIZING ground all our settings with as much location work as possible, and then we augmented and replaced." Key structures in the miniaturized city were staged around the production base at Pinewood Toronto Studios.The design and feel of the community were based on real upscale developments in Toronto, which had a planned community feel. We worked with an urban planner who introduced us to the rules of master-planned communities. That included real ratios of housing to commercial buildings and how much space would be devoted to housing versus commercial use, and then we modeled the world based on that." Leisureland structures reflected themes of conservation and micro-engineering. "The concept was that Leisureland was originally built by normal human-sized people," related Lindy De Quattro. They cleared the land and laid down subfloors, like you would for an office building. We imagined the substructure consisted of tiles beneath which they laid wiring, plumbing and other infrastructure, and on top of that they landscaped. It was a familiar structure to us at ILM because our San Francisco studio has something similar: we have underground parking, and then on top of that there is insulating material, and then on top of that they planted the parki Leisureland structures were designed in consideration of techniques used to mass-produce products for miniature residents. We discussed if Leisureland buildings should have wood-grain structure that suggested over-sized trees, or if they had grown fields of miniaturized trees, and we decided on the latter. Ditto food. The fabric for clothing that people wear in Leisureland was smallscale, as well, because it was woven on small looms by small people. 6 / 29 ILM visual effects art director Thang Le oversaw a nine-month process of designing

DOWNSIZING Leisureland and its support structures in collaboration with Stefania Cella and art director Doug Meerdink. "Alexander often remarked that he wanted Leisureland to feel like jail," said De Quattro. 'The occupants are in this walled area with protective netting over their heads, so even though it presents itself as a utopian society, it's a prison of their own making. Stefania Cella had already done groundwork to lay out the infrastructure, the main axis of the freeways and the broad strokes of residential neighborhoods. We built from that, knowing that Alexander didn't want us to make stuff up completely." The ovalshaped community spanned seven by five miles, encompassing networks of roadways, varieties of up-scale housing, and support-staff suburbs, all derived from photo and lidar surveys of houses that ILM rebuilt in 3D and propagated around the city. Color palettes took inspiration from modern shopping communities. "Alexander's 'banal' comment was mostly directed at the commercial area. He was really, deeply, personally offended by the ubiquitous mini-mall architectural styles. We looked at reference of The Grove in L.A., Westwood Village, the Americana in Glendale, Las Vegas and Palm Springs, and it was amazing how similar the architecture, signage and color palettes were among those malls. To Alexander, I think, that represented a lot of flaws in our society." Rodeo FX used ILM's enormous Leisureland model to generate environment extensions. "We referred to Leisureland as a 'non-renderable' asset," noted Rodeo FX visual effects supervisor Ara Khanikian. ¿The city was so huge, there was no way to generate every detail in high resolution; we had to treat it like an asset that we could quickly access. We worked closely with Lindy and her team at ILM and generated key shots of the 7 / 29 city using the model to create layouts and compositions. This step allowed us to quickly

DOWNSIZING design shots and accurately assess the level of detail that was needed. ILM provided us with the main Leisureland asset. We then updated every piece using high-res or mediumres CG assets, which enabled us to accurately light scenes in CG. We then either rendered a still frame and painted over that, or we generated technical passes from the CG and the painters enhanced textures without modifying the lighting. The camera was often not moving a great deal, and we had many static shots or nodal pans, which was fantastic for painting, but the lingering shots allowed the viewer to scrutinize every detail. odeo FX associate visual effects supervisor Laurent Gillet, CG supervisor FabLeisureland assets, including 129 buildings, which Rodeo FX compositing supervisor Julien Hery and his team layered into scenes with custom lawns, vegetation and landscaping. Full CG builds included the city's retaining wall - a 50-foot-tall concrete structure that appeared 700 feet high to downsized-human scale - a slowly rotating scenic Ferris wheel based on the London Eye, and an overhead gondola transportation network strung between towers that supported anti-predator netting.iWe went through rounds of concepts for the net," remarked Lindy De Quattro. "Stefania first gave us a sample of rigid metal material similar to a window screen, with a very fine, two-millimetersquare mesh. The idea was that it prevented insects and birds from picking off the little people. In our bidding phase, we discussed if the netting would need to move, or blow in the wind, which would have required simulations in every shot. By keeping it rigid, we 8 / 29 reasoned the net would move very little, and so we built from Stefania's sample and

DOWNSIZING plugged that into our shots. But that was not at all what Alexander imagined. He wanted the net to have more of a feeling of mosquito netting, non-metallic, and much more diaphanous, only visible when it was seen obliquely. So, we redesigned that with sagging and pinching where it gathered at each polei Omnipresent netting required a dexterous approach.iGenerating a single giant cloth sim to cover the whole city with netting would have been too huge and unwieldy," said De Quattro, iso we simulated the net's end position to get the proper draping, isolated sections and then either animated cloth motion, or used compositing tricks to give it motion. It was very challenging to give the netting the right look without its being too distracting. When they were doing the sound mix, Alexander suggested a little wind blowing through shots, so we simulated a ripple through the netting to give it life. The first example of human downsizing is revealed when Doctor Asbjørnsen, miniaturized, addresses a lecture hall audience atop a lectern. The Third Floor previsualized the scene using motion capture reference. "Alexander wore the suit," recalled Jourdan Biziou. ¿We went into a dance rehearsal space, set out markers on the floor and Alexander read the lines and performed as Asbjørnsen. We took measurements and recorded him with witness cams and audio, brought that into Maya and applied that to our animation rigs. Addison Bath, our head of research and development, wrote scripts for Maya to connect locators, calculate distances and focal lengths and render out slate elements. That process allowed Alexander to focus on dramatic blocking, while Jamie explored measurements for shooting the podium, placing the bluescreen, and directing eyelines 9 / 29 in the lecture hall."

DOWNSIZING Rodeo FX assembled elements of Asbjørnsen and another small-scaled element of the first community of downsized volunteers, who are wheeled out on a gurney. The production staged the gurney element with performers on a static set piece.iWe simulated gurney motion by moving the camera in toward them," explained Lindy De Quattro. "The problem was the actors were on scaffolding about 12 feet off the ground and the camera was quite heavy, so as it shot forward it shook the scaffolding. We managed to get the shot by taking all the grip equipment we had on set and jamming it up against the scaffolding with grips holding on to steady iti At Paul and Audrey's college reunion, the couple are amazed to see Paul's old acquaintance Dave and Dave's wife Carol (Maribeth Monroe) downsized, transported to their table in a transparent carry-box. "That was one of our most complicated shots," remarked Jamie Price. ¿We knew we needed real performances of the actors in the box. We planned to shoot the full-scale element first, with the actor playing Dave's brother carrying a prop box containing five-inch-tall dolls for reference. We put markers on the box and then tracked the box to a 14-times-bigger box on a motion base, and we shot that with a giant motion control setup using cable-flown Spydercam. What was challenging about that was the scale. The shot required Dave's brother to bring Dave and Carol close to camera, and then move away. Multiplying that 10-foot walk by 14 times required a run of 140 feet, but we didn't have a stage big enough to place an oversized box containing our actors in the center and then fly the camera past. Instead, we simulated the box's motion by pushing in, and then we twisted the motion base and pulled back to 10 / 29 simulate rotation on the boxii

DOWNSIZING he Third Floor choreographed the complex interplay of motions. Mr. A then anT was scaled down by 1/14," stated Mr. X previs supervisor Chris de Souza. "To shoot a miniaturized person with a small camera up close, two feet away and four feet high, we extrapolated that to be 14 times larger, shooting with the camera further back and higher. I did some of those translations live on set, but mostly I worked beforehand to do all the translations between the big and small cameras, so when we got to set Jamie knew where to put markers for the cameras. Mr. X's data allowed ILM location matchmover Duncan Blackman to plot motions for translating the camera move to the Spydercam and oversized carry-box. I tracked the camera move and re-engineered that motion to eliminate the translation and the rotation on the box. We retained Y-rotation so that the camera could move forward and then back away. All the rest of the rotations were on the gimbal and the box." Translating one-foot-cube motions to the 14-square-foot box revealed unexpected hazards. "We started by putting stunt people in the gimbal box to see what the motion looked like," recalled Lindy De Quattro. "As it turned out, if you hold something in your hands and walk across the room, you shake the crap out of that object. If we'd scaled that up appropriately and put it on a rig, we would've killed the actors. The production cast Steadicam camera operator Michael Heathcote in the role of Dave's brother to ensure an even hand transported the carry-box on location.iWe translated that motion to the gimbal and jiggered it so we could put as much of the motion onto the camera as I1 / 29 possible. As the camera flew into the box, we controlled the roll and tilt and dampened

the motion until it was safe for the actors. DOWNSIZING Tricky Guy VFX supplied a 10-foot hydraulic motion base and playback and recording systems developed with Concept Overdrive motion control specialist Steven Rosenbluth. "The motion base works by chasing a target," explained motion base supervisor Andrew Verhoeven. "Lindy and Jamie had worked out a very specific move and we matched the speed by making the changes in position occur faster. The Spydercam had to follow a super smooth, slow move into the actors in the box as the box turned in space and the camera gave the illusion of travel. It had to be frame-accurate, so we had all our server loops amped up so high they were ready to jump. ILM programmed the moves in Maya, which we constrained to the motion base, working out reverse kinematics by taking Cartesian coordinates and translating those in real time to the motion base. Rodeo FX assembled elements. "They lined up perfectly," stated Ara Khanikian. "It was really well shot. In the composite, we made sure to add back micro jitters and movements that they had smoothed out on the gimbal. And then, we created glass reflections in the box. In one distant shot, we added tiny digi-doubles of Dave and Carol, but all the other shots were achieved with composite elements.i Big/small juxtapositions continue as Paul and Tracy investigate a Leisureland showroom, where a tiny salesman (Neil Patrick Harris) play-acts in a model home with his glamorous wife (Laura Dern). The production built a miniature prop mansion that opened like a doll's house, and shot elements of Harris and Dern in a two-tiered partial set. Rodeo FX replaced the prop with a CG house, dressed with appropriate levels of detail, 12 / 29 and composited performers into the mansion, which they integrated to assist closure of

hinged walls. where Paul eyes a downsized resident Margo T Floor prevised the scene, ILM plotted elements, and Rodeo FA assembled composites. "We shot the big people on a real bus," related Lindy De Quattro. "The little people were on a stage in Toronto in one of the little passenger boxes, which seated 16 people, and we put that on a pneumatic rigi The production art department supplied a SketchUp file of the passenger cubicle, which Mr. X converted into a Maya file techvis and ILM used to plot perspectives. "In wider shots, with many boxes in frame, we shot eight plates from different angles. We kept track of who was sitting where and which box they were in, and then we solved the camera perspective for each box. We used a laser to figure out where each camera should be on the stage floor and then shot angles from a scissor lifti The downsizing procedure requires Paul and Audrey to remove all hair and dental work. Production makeup department head Julie Hewitt collaborated with Matt Damon's makeup artist, Christine Beveridge, and prosthetic supplier Stephen Bettles to simulate a hairless, shaved appearance. Lola VFX visual effects supervisor Edson Williams oversaw digital cosmetics. "We couldn't shave Matt's hair for reasons of scheduling and logistics," noted Susan MacLeod. 'The makeup team applied prosthetic baldness effects. Visual effects simulated removal of Matt's arm-hair, eyebrows and eyelashes. Kirsten wore a bald cap beneath a hoodie. We touched that up digitally, scaling down the shape of the hair DOWNSIZING 'he Safraneks next encounter miniature people on a bus ride to Leisureland where Paul eyes a downsized resident (Margo Martindale), one of many tiny passengers in a tier of tiny cubicles adjacent to the full-scale seats. The Third 13 / 29

DOWNSIZING piled up beneath the bald cap, and removed one eyebrow." Downsizing is detailed in a sequence that leads to a white-walled chamber where nurses wheel Paul and other nude anesthetized males on gurneys and, after irradiation, scoop them, tiny-sized, from their beds. The production filmed nurses using metal spatulas to maneuver small weighted beanbags representing each tiny sleeping man. ILM oversaw performer scans with scale-appropriate attention to detail. "It was my first day on set," recalled Lindy De Quattro. "When I arrived, there were 24 naked men walking around trying to find their marks. I took a seat next to Alexander and his cinematographer, Phedon Papamichael, and his wife who happened to be visiting that day, and we sat at the video monitor while they filmed take after take of naked men. We labeled each naked man, so we knew who was in what bed, scanned them for modeling and textures, and re-created them exactly. We first arrayed the tiny bodies very perfectly centered, but we decided that wasn't plausible. As each man shrank, we decided different parts of their bodies caught on parts of the beds, causing them to end up in funny poses, which added to the comedy of the scene." ILM tactfully generated anatomically correct digi-doubles. Matt Damon was the only one who was not naked when we scanned him," said De Quattro. "As the star, he got to wear a little thong, and so we had to borrow his manhood from one of the other actors who had the closest skin tone. That led to more conversations with Alexander, discussing if the penis was too small or too big, should it be sticking up, or should it be tucked between Paul's legs? We didn't want to offend Matt, but we also didn't want it to grab the 14 / 29 audience's attention. We went somewhere in the middle." Characters were animated with

realistic dynamic muscle simulations. "We relied on sims to get them to slide off the spatulas and have their flesh squish out in contact with the different surfaces, but we keyframe-animated each character." room scene using an oversized saltine prop. Atomic Fiction adjusted textures of the cellophane wrapper to create scale-appropriate wrinkling. The filmmakers relied on in-camera techniques to lend a feel of miniature scale to the room. The recovery room was entirely a live-action set," stated Jamie Price. "One of the things that makes an audience perceive something as miniature is a lack of detail, and there was a conscious effort made to simplify the detail of certain sets. After Paul's transition, we kept that recovery room set spartan and simple. Stunned by Audrey's betrayal, Paul is escorted to his Leisureland mansion via an electric ride-share vehicle. The production filmed Paul's ride in a Toronto housing district. Rodeo FX provided environment embellishments. "Outside the transition center," related Ara Khanikian, "we retained the foreground plate. Everything beyond that was a CG environment. As they pass through what looks like a miniature Venice and the camera panned out across the city, Jamie shot an environment in Toronto to capture the timing of hero cars in the foreground, but we ended up re-creating that environment. We retained only part of the road with the ride-share vehicle. Leisureland was supposed to be DOWNSIZING pon waking, Paul is alarmed to learn that his wife has opted out of downsizing, and a nurse (Natasha Bromfield) attempts to alleviate Paul's grief by offering him a giant, human-scale saltine cracker. The production staged the recovery 15 / 29

DOWNSIZING about 10 years old, so we had to rework the look of Toronto streets to remove impertections and make them appear very manicured.i Leisureland traffic featured CG assets that Rodeo FX developed in Side Effects Houdini using procedural animation controls to alter speed, frequency, vehicle suspension, digi-double drivers and traffic lights. "We had four-wheel and three-wheel ride-shares, buses and gondolas. Our procedural tools allowed us to drop in assets and automate all the background traffic, gondolas, and the Ferris wheeli Paul attends a garden party at Dave Johnson's palatial home where the walls of Leisureland loom above the festivities. Shade VFX supplied environment extensions to the Toronto location, making use of ILM elements.iWe art directed the height, texture and lighting of the wall from shot to shot, commented Shade VFX supervisor Mitch Drain. iSometimes when you do things that are photographically correct, they're not necessarily dramatically correct and that was the case with the wall, houses and trees in the surrounding area. The netting over Leisureland also required a lot of art direction to determine how much it moved and how it cast shadows on the wall. In Lucasfilm and Walt Disney Pictures' follow-up, Star Wars: The Last Jedi, writer and director Rian Johnson continued to build on the mythology, taking the baton from director J.J. Abrams to delve into mysteries of Luke's monastic retreat and the fate of the Jedi Order. Luke's Force-strong sister, General Leia Organa (Carrie Fisher), continues to lead the Resistance against the fascistic First Order, aided by Vice Admiral Holdo (Laura Dern), Commander Poe Dameron (Oscar Isaac) and former stormtrooper, Finn (John Boyega). restrictions in terms of where the story had to go, said Rian Johnson, best known for THE LAST JEDI his indie drama Brick, and the science fiction thriller Looper. "It was really a matter of more, more, more." 'More' translated to an effects shot tally of 2,106 shots, and was driven by a commitment by show producers D.B. Weiss and David Benioff to make Game of Thrones bigger and better with each season. "Dan and David have said that there is an unspoken pact with the fan base that the show will top itself with each season," noted Bauer. "The fan base expects it and the producers want to meet those expectations. But even beyond that, the narrative demands more spectacle with each season because the fantastical elements of the story have increased over time. There are more battles, and the sizes of the armies keeps increasing. The army of the dead increases because whoever they kill 1 / 43 joins them. We're also adding giants to that army. The dragons are growing, doubling

GAME OF THRONES in size, as well. All of these story elements have led to more spectacle with each season. Beyond all of that, though, I think the producers have been emboldened by our success with the visual effects, and that inspires them to want to put more visual effects into the show." Not surprisingly, given the ambitious nature of the season, the Season 7 shoot was longer than those for previous seasons, extending from August 25, 2016 until February 28, 2017. Throughout that period, the show ran multiple units that ventured out from the production's base in Belfast, Northern Ireland, to locations that included Iceland, Croatia, Canada and Spain. "We always have two full first units," explained visual effects producer Steve Kullback, a veteran of the series since Season 2, "sometimes in different countries, and it is not unusual to have splinter units running with one or both. around the world.
